meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You only live once, but if you do it right, once is enough'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mae West. Quote Investigator traces the joke to comedian Joe E. Lewis (1952); Wikiquote lists the Mae West version as Misattributed.

answer.label: Not Mae West — a nightclub comedian's joke
answer.sourceLine: This is a stage one-liner, not a Mae West epigram. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the joke to comedian Joe E. Lewis, quoted in a 1952 Hedda Hopper column as “You only live once, but if you work it right, once is enough.” The familiar “do it right” wording is a later floating variant, and Mae West only became attached to it on the modern internet — Wikiquote ↗ files it under “Misattributed.”

source.excerpt: You only live once, but if you do it right, once is enough.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the “once is enough” joke to Joe E. Lewis, quoted opening at the Mocambo in a 1952 column: “You only live once, but if you work it right, once is enough.”
By 1965 Frank Sinatra used a version of the line and said he “stole that from Joe E. Lewis” — further evidence the gag belongs to Lewis, not Mae West, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the Mae West version only in its “Misattributed” section, with no primary source in her work.

The bare phrase “You only live once” is far older — Quote Investigator finds it in an 1896 English translation of Balzac’s La Comédie Humaine — but the punch-line “once is enough” is the 1950s comic addition.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented form, from a 1952 Hedda Hopper column, reads “if you work it right” and names Joe E. Lewis. The “do it right” phrasing that circulates under Mae West’s name is a later variant — Quote Investigator ↗ records it as a 2011 high-school class motto.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no single identifiable published source: the underlying joke is a Joe E. Lewis stage line first documented in a 1952 newspaper column, while the specific “do it right” variant is a later, floating paraphrase. Because the wording’s origin is an unfixed spoken gag rather than a datable published work, no copyright status can be asserted.

author.name: Joe E. Lewis
author.kicker: The real source of the joke
author.heading: Joe E. Lewis
author.bio: Joe E. Lewis (born Joseph Klewan, 1902–1971) was an American nightclub comedian and singer who became one of the highest-paid saloon entertainers of his era. Once a crooner, he was left with a scarred throat and gravelly voice after gangsters slashed him in 1927 for refusing to renew a contract at a Capone-linked Chicago club — a story told in his 1955 biography and the 1957 Frank Sinatra film The Joker Is Wild. His hard-living, quick-witted stage persona made him the natural home for the “you only live once… once is enough” gag.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s classic feel-good misattributions: a witty one-liner pinned to Mae West because it sounds like her, when the documented trail leads to a nightclub comedian.

items.why: Quotation databases, memes, and merchandise credit the line to Mae West, but no Mae West film, play, screenplay, or interview is known to contain it. Wikiquote ↗ places it firmly in the “Misattributed” section.

items.scope: The documented source of the joke
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest instance in a 1952 Hedda Hopper column: “Joe E. Lewis, who opens at the Mocambo June 3, says, ‘You only live once, but if you work it right, once is enough.’” Frank Sinatra later used the line and credited Lewis outright.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Joe E. Lewis’s (documented 1952, “work it right”); the “do it right” Mae West version is a modern misattribution, per Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Mae West
lead: Mae West built her whole persona on exactly this kind of double-edged wisecrack about living large, so a punchy line about making one life count slid neatly under her name once the internet started matching quotes to famous faces rather than to sources.
The real author, Joe E. Lewis, was a Prohibition-era saloon comic whose fame faded after the 1950s — a less ‘quotable’ name for a meme. The line survived; the attribution drifted to the bigger star.
context.pull: The joke is Lewis’s. The fame is West’s. The internet swapped one for the other.
